title: Sixth triage draw of twenty untriaged, unrun, governed-risk suites; the draw concentrates in Home and Tower, and two of its byte-scanning cases are proven vacuous against the very defect they name

scope.drawnFrom: governedRiskFiles from scripts/quality/test-ci-coverage-census.mjs, rows with untriaged true and covered false, band before score before path. The draw itself was fixed when T-479 was filed at base 2b942ee94; this record judges that same twenty at base 538ce854a.
scope.disjointnessIsAsserted: src/__tests__/behaviors/t479-stale-suite-triage-record.test.ts reads all six sibling records and fails if any path appears in two of the seven. T-742's own guard checked four; this one checks all six that precede it, including t475, which no prior guard in this family read.
scope.poolReconciliationNotDone: T-479's acceptance carries `before drawing anything further, reconcile T-742's +38` -- re-running the census at 5cb905487 with node_modules installed from that base's own lockfile, to settle whether 55 or 93 is the right pool figure. That precondition governs a SEVENTH draw, not this record's triage of an already-fixed twenty, and it is NOT discharged here. It is still owed, and no `remaining` figure is published in this record precisely because every such figure inherits that unsettled answer. Whoever takes the seventh draw must settle it first.

jestEvidence.how: Each of the twenty was executed on its own with `npx jest --runTestsByPath <path> --no-coverage --ci --json --outputFile`, and every count in suites[] is read out of that run's JSON by scripts/../build-record.mjs rather than typed. --runTestsByPath is used for all twenty because four paths contain the parenthesised segment (maestro), which jest would read as a regex group.
jestEvidence.executedAt: 2026-09-25T23:09Z to 2026-09-25T23:18Z, before any verdict below was written
jestEvidence.harnessFoundTests: Asserted rather than assumed: every one of the twenty runs reports numTotalTestSuites 1, exactly one entry in testResults whose name ends with the path asked for, and numTotalTests greater than zero. A run that matched no file exits green and reports zero, which is the failure a green exit code hides.

mutationEvidence.how: Each proof mutates the SUBJECT -- a route, a component, a page -- never the suite under judgement, applies the mutation, re-runs that one suite to JSON, and restores the file. Before and after counts below are read from the two run JSONs.
mutationEvidence.whyBothKindsAreRecorded: A mutation that kills proves the suite can fail. A mutation that SURVIVES is the more valuable finding and this record publishes it as a first-class result rather than as an absence: M3 and M4 each destroy the exact property their case is named for and leave the suite green. Recording only kills would make a blind detector indistinguishable from a healthy one.

proofs.proves: VACUOUS. All three cases stay green while the leak the case is named for is live, because the case asserts a COMMENT is present and that one particular wrong spelling is absent. This is the 6ebe6d4a9 defect shape, found alive in a suite nothing runs.

drawConcentration.whyItMatters: Every row in the pool at this base is band high, score 10, signal tenant_scoped_read, so the ranking collapses to path order and the draw is an alphabetical sweep rather than a risk-ordered spread. Unlike T-742, which put nineteen of twenty in one directory, this draw spreads across eleven directories -- but it is still concentrated in two products: eight rows are Home surfaces and route handlers, ten are Tower. A reader told `twenty suites, highest governed risk first` should read that as: the untriaged residue in this repo is now Home and Tower, and both are surfaces a signed-in executive reads. The per-directory breakdown is published so the concentration cannot be understated by a record edited after the fact.

populationsDeclared.sourceTextScanner: FIRED -- 4 of 20 rows carry sourceTextScanner true, and every one of them is judged rewrite_as_behavior rather than wired. T-742's draw contained zero scanners and its guard therefore declared that control VACUOUS; this draw is the opposite case, so the declaration states the count and the guard recomputes it from the rows. A declaration that cannot be wrong in both directions is not a control: it must be falsifiable by a draw with no scanners AND by a draw whose count is understated.
populationsDeclared.redSuites: FIRED -- 3 of 20 rows are not green, and each carries a verdict that does not assume it passes. T-742's draw contained zero red suites and declared that control VACUOUS. The two are not symmetric in what they mean: a red suite here is evidence the suite still has an opinion about a product that moved, and both of this draw's red suites turned out to be stale fixtures rather than live defects -- one a brand rename, one a deliberate roster narrowing.
populationsDeclared.vacuousCasesFound: FIRED -- 2 of the 5 mutation proofs SURVIVED, on rows 2 and 15. Neither suite was red; both would have been wired into CI on a green run alone. This is the population no prior record in this family has declared, and it is the reason mutationEvidence is part of the record rather than a note in a pull request.

forbiddenEdits: No file judged in suites[] is edited by this item. Every mutation in mutationEvidence was applied to a subject file and restored; `git status --porcelain` was clean after each. The triage records a verdict and hands it on; wiring, rewriting, updating and repair are the follow-on items' work.

followOnItems.T-480: Wire the fourteen suites this record judges wire_into_ci into a named CI scope, so a run reports whether they pass. Each is green at this base with nothing skipped, and none is a source-text scanner. Wiring alone; no suite is edited.
followOnItems.T-481: Rewrite the four source-text scanners as behavioral proofs: rows 1, 2, 13 and 18. Row 14 is the worked example -- it asserts by composition exactly what row 13 asserts by regex, on the same route. Row 2 must be rewritten against mutation M4 and row 18 against the same class: the replacement must go red when the property is destroyed by a re-spelling, not merely by a deletion.
followOnItems.T-482: Update row 12's honest-timeout assertion from the retired Atlas brand to the product's current agent name, recording #4037 as the reason, and keep the wording-quality and length assertions it was written for.
followOnItems.T-483: Row 15: refresh the outcome-report fixture identity to one that can actually reach the same-client admin fallback under the post-6ebe6d4a9 roster, WITHOUT widening CANONICAL_CLIENT_ADMIN_EMAILS, then re-run mutation M3 and require the widening case to go red. It passes vacuously today.
followOnItems.T-484: Replace the four byte-matching cases sitting inside suites this record wires into CI -- two in row 4, one in row 12, one in row 20 -- with assertions over behavior. They are named individually in partialSourceTextCaseNames so they cannot be lost inside a green suite.

suites.rationale: Every one of the seven cases reads a component file with fs.readFileSync and asserts substrings of it; nothing here renders, calls or imports the surface it names. Two cases are already red, and both failed on a string the product legitimately re-spelled rather than on a boundary that broke: the case asserting "CXO readout" appears in ChapterPage.tsx and the case asserting a literal useState initialiser line appears in HomeV4App.tsx. That is the failure mode a byte-scan has instead of a defect report, and it is why wiring this into CI as it stands would block merges on rewording. Rewrite the boundary it means -- Home stays on the v4 canvas and does not reach Admin's surfaces -- as a render or import-graph assertion.
failingCaseNames: Home/Admin boundary contract :: keeps context and architecture inside the approved v4 Home canvas
Home/Admin boundary contract :: keeps Home preview first render deterministic for hydration

suites.rationale: All three cases are regexes over component source. Mutation M4 in this record's mutationProofs is the decisive one: the case named `keeps raw evidence identifiers off the executive Home surface` asserts that a JSDoc COMMENT is present in src/components/home/v4/source-label.ts and that one particular wrong spelling is absent. Replacing the governed summary with `ids: evidenceIds.map(String).join(", ")` -- raw internal evidence ids on the CXO sidenote, the exact leak the case is named for -- left all three cases green. This is the shape of the defect that went ten weeks unnoticed at 6ebe6d4a9: a control proved by its own name appearing in the file. It must not be wired; it must be rewritten to render the sidenote and assert what a reader sees.

Renders the /home route component for each reviewed Home tenant through the governed ECL projection and asserts what comes back, including that an unsupported active tenant name is not shown over the default bundle. Three cases, all green, nothing skipped, and each names a tenant-scoped read rather than a file's bytes.

Five of the seven cases assert a filesystem fact -- that a deleted /home/* re-export route has not been reintroduced -- which is the right instrument for that claim, and mutation M2a proved it decisive: adding src/app/(maestro)/home/data-trust/page.tsx turned the suite red on exactly that case. The remaining two scan component source for banned copy; mutation M2b showed they fail on a phrase inserted as a COMMENT, so they read bytes rather than rendered copy and a differently-computed string would pass them. Wire the suite -- it is green and its structural cases can fail -- and hand the two byte-matching cases to T-484 rather than leaving them to look like copy proofs.
partialSourceTextCaseNames: no /home/* re-exports of /admin/* pages :: keeps Home copy tenant-scoped and free of setup/admin framing
no /home/* re-exports of /admin/* pages :: keeps visible Home entry copy aligned to Admin instead of setup-era labels

suites.rationale: Drives the /api/home/know/ask route and asserts the visible answer contract on two failure paths: answer-construction language leaking into final prose, and a terminal blocked answer when the streaming read fails. Both green, both about what a caller receives.

Asserts the ask route answers from the same served Home bundle source that renders the page, and that the reviewed fallback stays visible to the API caller. Two green cases over the route's real response, not its text.

One green case: canonical Home tenant aliases are authorized through the app client key. It mocks @/lib/auth/tenancy wholesale, so it proves the route CALLS the fence with a particular argument and nothing about whether the fence holds -- its sibling suite (row 8) exists for that reason and carries the behavioral proof. Wire it for what it does assert, and do not read a green run here as tenancy evidence.

The boundary suite this draw was told to start from. It mocks the identity layer BELOW requireTenancy and runs the real fence, and mutation M1 proved the assertion can fail: dropping requestedClientKey from the route's requireTenancy call took it from 0 failing to 4 failing of 9, including the foreign-alias refusal and the positive same-tenant case. Nine green cases covering refusal before any document is produced, both export formats, and the requested-versus-active tenant label. An unrun fence and a vacuous fence look identical from outside; this one is not vacuous, and nothing runs it.

Asserts /api/tower/seed-demo blocks demo seeding and demo reset for governed foundation tenants BEFORE the role or write lookup -- ordering, not just outcome, which is the property that matters for a destructive operator route. Two green cases.

Two green cases: the Tower ask prompt inherits the shared consultant answer shape, and the legacy ask path keeps the selected Tower tenant candidate set. Both exercise the composed value rather than the route file's bytes.
One green case asserting /api/tower/chat resolves the Tower answer context under the SELECTED client key. Small, but it is the tenant-selection seam and it runs the route.

Red on one case of four. The route's honest-timeout copy was renamed from the Atlas brand to aVa in #4037 (`aVa could not complete that response in time. Try again or pick a narrower question.`), and the case still asserts /Atlas/. The intent behind the assertion -- that the timeout clears the thinking state in CXO-grade wording rather than a generic error string -- is intact and is worth keeping; only the brand token is stale. Update the expectation to the product's current agent name, record #4037 as the reason, and keep the length and /time/i assertions. The fourth case reads route.ts and asserts substrings, so it carries the same byte-scan weakness as rows 1, 2, 13 and 18 and goes to T-484.

failingCaseNames: Tower synthesis Fix C levers :: emits an honest user-facing timeout message instead of silence

suites.rationale: All six cases are regexes over the route's source, read once at module load. It is a better scanner than most -- it strips block and line comments first, so it cannot be satisfied by a comment carrying the banned name, which is precisely the trick that beat a gate at 6ebe6d4a9. It is still a scanner: `expect(routeCode).toMatch(/loadTenantTowerPortfolio/)` proves the identifier is written in the file, not that the portfolio load is tenant-scoped at run time, and `toMatch(/clientKey/)` plus `toMatch(/cacheKey/)` proves neither that the cache key contains the tenant nor that it is used. The invariants it names are real and severe -- one tenant's synthesis served to another -- which is why they deserve a behavioral proof rather than wiring as they stand.

Nine green cases that CALL composeAtlasSynthesisUserMessage and assert the composed message: the tenant display name in the header for three tenants, an honest empty state that is never another tenant's content, and snapshot cases pinning that an unknown tenant gets an honest empty rather than a silent default. This is the behavioral form of what row 13 asserts by regex, on the same route, which makes the pair a ready-made example for T-481.

Red on two cases of four, and the cause is a deliberate narrowing rather than a regression: commit 6ebe6d4a9 replaced the demo sign-in roster, cutting CANONICAL_CLIENT_ADMIN_EMAILS from ten persona addresses to the two real AbarVa admin addresses. The fixture identity in this suite is one of the ten that were removed and carries primaryRole client_viewer, so it can no longer satisfy isSameClientAdminFallback and the route answers 403 where the suite expects 200. The route is correct and tighter; the fixture is stale. It must not be repaired by widening the roster. Worse, mutation M3 shows a second case is now VACUOUS: dropping the same-client condition from isSameClientAdminFallback -- destroying the very guard the case is named for -- left `does not let a same-client fallback widen into another requested client` green and the suite failing on the same two cases as before, because an identity that can never be admin-like never reaches the fallback at all. Update the fixture to an identity that does reach it, then re-run M3 and require the widening case to go red.
failingCaseNames: GET /api/v1/tower/outcome-report :: streams DOCX for a same-client admin fallback when the active-client cookie is missing
GET /api/v1/tower/outcome-report :: streams XLSX for a same-client admin fallback when the active-client cookie is missing

suites.rationale: Renders AiSuccessCommandCenter and asserts the generated advisory story and architecture canvas, that expanded Ask aVa is wired to the Home KNOW provider with export-capable rendering, and that internal provider errors do not reach the drawer. Three green cases, all over rendered output.

Four green cases over the AI ops cost ledger: it emits a variance alert when realized cost exceeds projection by more than ten percent with no reason code, suppresses it when a reason code is on file, and builds an estimated ledger from the license-dollar layer until live run-cost fields exist. Computed outcomes, not text.

Eighty-eight cases, every one a regex over five files read at module load -- two loader scripts, the Tower reader, the command-center view model and its types. It is the largest and most brittle scanner in this draw, and its assertions are exact expressions: `gating_constraint: row.gating_constraint`, `gatingConstraint: item.gatingConstraint ?? null`. Any legitimate refactor breaks it, and any re-spelled leak passes it -- M4 on row 2 demonstrates that direction on a smaller case. What it pins is genuinely important and hard-won (an unrecorded number is not zero; readiness must not fall back to an adoption rate and then to a literal), which is the argument for giving it a real instrument: run the projection and the view model over fixtures and assert the values that come out. Eighty-eight green byte-matches are not eighty-eight proofs.
Fifteen green cases over the current-layer answer path, exercising the computed answer rather than its source. The largest purely behavioral suite in the draw after row 14.

Three of the four cases call readTowerEclProjectionPreview and assert it degrades to null instead of throwing when rows or the tenant key are absent, and still returns a preview when rows are present -- the positive case that keeps the negatives from being vacuous. The fourth slices the /tower page source at the call site and matches /\.catch\(\(\) => null\)/, which proves the text of one call and would pass a try/catch or a wrapper written any other way. Wire the suite; hand that one case to T-484.
